headline: AI firm hiring 'literal pirate' for up to $500,000/year to salvage ancient shipwrecks
summary: AE Studio is leveraging AI to sift through 80 million pages of historical records to pinpoint lost Spanish colonial shipwrecks, offering a unique, high-paying role for experienced seafarers.
details: AE Studio, an AI research firm, is seeking a "literal pirate" to salvage ancient shipwrecks located by its AI. The role offers a compensation package up to $500,000 annually, including equity and a share of recovered treasure. This unique job combines advanced AI with hands-on maritime exploration.

The position demands extensive nautical experience, diving certifications for "conditions insurance companies decline to cover," and proficiency in handling permits and port bureaucracy. Bonus qualifications include pre-1800 salvage experience and operational experience in high-risk maritime regions.

Compensation is structured like 17th-century privateer commissions, with equity in a new venture, cash heavily weighted toward upside, and a share of the plunder. AE Studio will cover logistics and legal costs for the treasure hunter.

The firm's AI analyzes 80 million pages of Spanish colonial records spanning five centuries, including nautical, admiralty, and insurance writings. This data helps identify areas most likely to contain undiscovered shipwrecks and their valuable cargo.

Since "the model does not swim," the hired buccaneer will perform the actual search and recovery operations. The job listing, though whimsical, is real and part of AE Studio's Skunkworks division, known for unconventional projects.

topic: military tech blamed for civilian plane crash
headline_marked: [[GPS jamming by US military]] linked to fatal civilian plane crash in New Mexico
headline: GPS jamming by US military linked to fatal civilian plane crash in New Mexico
summary: A medevac plane crashed in New Mexico, killing all four aboard, after a US military GPS jamming exercise disrupted navigation systems. This marks the first US civilian crash attributed to electronic warfare.
details: In May, a Beechcraft King Air medevac plane crashed in New Mexico, killing two pilots and two nurses. The accident occurred during a US military GPS jamming exercise at White Sands Missile Range, which rendered modern navigation systems unusable for the aircraft.

Pilots were forced to rely on older, less familiar navigation methods, leading to disorientation and the crash into a mountain. This incident is the first confirmed US civilian plane crash linked to GPS jamming.

The military had issued notices for at least 10 such GPS jamming exercises in the past year. Experts warn that as drone and electronic warfare expand, navigation disruptions are increasingly affecting civilian aviation far beyond conflict zones.

Medevac flights are inherently dangerous, often operating on short notice into unfamiliar airstrips and sometimes in marginal weather. The crew on this flight, Captain Keelan Clark (30) and First Officer Ali Kawsara (23), had limited experience in their roles.

Modern cockpits use GPS-enabled RNAV systems for easy navigation, even in low visibility. Before GPS, pilots relied on magnetic compasses and ground-based radio beacons, requiring complex 3D mental mapping and extensive practice.

The pilots took off in clear but moonless conditions, with few visual references in the rural area. The loss of GPS forced them to revert to these older, more challenging methods, contributing to the fatal disorientation.
